title: The Wire That Breathes

location.name: Westminster High School (weather point); applies to every overhead line in the radius

one_liner: Power lines are rated as if every hour were a hot, windless afternoon, so most hours they could safely carry far more, and on the worst heat hours the fixed rating isn't safe enough.
problem: Most overhead lines carry a fixed static rating that assumes about 40 C air, almost no wind and full sun all year. The real limit is how hot the wire gets, which depends on the weather. Clean energy waits years for grid room while existing wires sit under-used.
fix: Rate each line hour by hour from real weather (dynamic line rating). It frees capacity on wires that already exist with no construction, and flags heat-wave hours when the fixed rating is too generous.
shock_line: The wires aren't full. We just pretend every hour is a hot, still afternoon, and on the one afternoon that really is, the fixed number isn't even safe.

title: The Pilot That Never Flew (Stanton, 12 miles from Irvine)

location.name: SCE EPIC 'Advanced Technology Dynamic Line Rating' pilot at Barre Substation, Stanton, Orange County (2015-2017). The line is not named in t

one_liner: Twelve miles from this room, Edison tried to let a power line 'breathe' and the project died because trees blocked the radio signal. The federal deadline to do it with weather data instead is December 17, 2026, 33 days from now.
problem: Southern California Edison planned a real dynamic line rating pilot that used Nexans/Valley Group CAT-1 tension monitors, with its radio antenna on the tower at Barre Substation in Stanton. The pilot was scheduled to run Dec 2015 to Dec 2016. It was cancelled before any construction because a line-of-sight survey found all three radio paths blocked by vegetation, and SCE concluded the technology was 'not practical' for its system. Ten years later the federal rules have changed. FERC Order 881 requires weather-adjusted (ambient-adjusted) ratings, and FERC gave CAISO until December 17, 2026 and SCE/SDG&E until October 15, 2027. That makes this a 'right now' story for a team pitching software-only line rating that needs no radios on towers. For scale, SCE's alternative is construction: West of Devers cost $740M to triple a corridor from 1,600 MW to 4,800 MW.
fix: See research/NICHE_CASES.md (map node values and upgrade potential).

stats.label: SCE's DLR pilot planned to install CAT-1 tension monitors (load cells, ambient temperature sensor and net radiation sensors) to compute real-time line ratings. Schedule: authority to proceed Jan 2, 2015; pilot operation Dec 19, 2015 to Dec 19, 2016; close-out by Feb 16, 2017.

The project was cancelled before equipment was installed. Poles M3-P4, M3-P7 and M4-P2 were surveyed for radio line-of-sight to an antenna on the transmission tower at Barre substation, and all three paths were obstructed by vegetation.

SCE's stated problem: its practice is fixed line ratings 'pre-calculated based on assumed-fixed conditions throughout the year'. Its conclusion: DLR 'with the current operating procedure is not practical' because long lines need many radio repeaters.

On April 30, 2025, FERC granted CAISO an extension to implement Order 881 (ambient-adjusted line ratings) from June 15, 2025 to December 17, 2026. It also extended the deadline for CAISO participating transmission owners (SCE, SDG&E and others) to October 15, 2027.

CAISO's Sept 1, 2026 release deck lists 'FERC 881 Track 3: AAR in Market Applications & EMS' with the note that the effective date of the Order 881 tariff is 'under internal review'. As of that date, weather-adjusted ratings were not yet live in CAISO's market software.

West of Devers Upgrade (SCE, completed May 2021): four 220 kV circuits on a 48-mile corridor between Devers (near Palm Springs), Vista (Grand Terrace) and San Bernardino substations. It raised capacity from 1,600 MW to 4,800 MW at a total cost of $740 million.

title: Eleven Minutes to Dark (Path 44 at San Onofre)

location.name: Path 44 (five 230 kV lines south of San Onofre) and the SONGS intertie separation scheme: September 8, 2011 Pacific Southwest blackout

one_liner: In 2011, the amps on five wires next to San Onofre crept from 5,900 to 9,500 while nobody was watching, and 2.7 million people went dark in eleven minutes.
problem: On a hot shoulder-season afternoon, September 8, 2011, a technician error tripped the Hassayampa-North Gila 500 kV line in Arizona at 3:27:39 p.m. Power rerouted north through Path 44, the five 230 kV lines at San Onofre, just 27 miles from Irvine. The amps climbed step by step (5,900, 6,700, 7,800) until they passed the 8,000-amp trigger of the San Onofre separation scheme, peaking near 9,500 amps. San Diego was cut off and collapsed, and both San Onofre nuclear units shut down. The cascade lasted about 11 minutes and left about 2.7 million customers without power, including all 1.4 million of SDG&E's. FERC and NERC blamed a lack of real-time awareness of system conditions, which is exactly the visibility a live line-rating dashboard provides. Accuracy note: the 8,000 A figure was a protection-scheme trip threshold, not a thermal sag rating.
fix: See research/NICHE_CASES.md (map node values and upgrade potential).
shock_line: In 2011, the amps on five wires next to San Onofre crept from 5,900 to 9,500 while nobody was watching, and 2.7 million people went dark in eleven minutes.

stats.label: Timeline: the Hassayampa-North Gila (H-NG) 500 kV line tripped at 15:27:39. The SONGS separation scheme operated at 15:38:21 and the island collapsed by 15:38:38, about 11 minutes total. H-NG had been at 78% of its normal rating beforehand, on 'a hot, shoulder season day'.

After H-NG tripped, flow on Path 44 rose 84%. Loading went from 5,900 to 6,700 to about 7,800 amps against the 8,000 amps needed to trigger the SONGS separation scheme, then exceeded the trip point and reached as high as 9,500 amps.
Load lost: SDG&E 4,293 MW (about 1.4 million customers); CFE Baja California 2,205 MW (about 1.1 million); IID 929 MW (about 146,000); APS 389 MW (about 70,000). SONGS nuclear units shut down.

The FERC/NERC staff report (released May 1, 2012) says the system was not being operated in a secure N-1 state, a failure stemming primarily from weaknesses in operations planning and real-time situational awareness; about 2.7 million customers lost power.

title: The Ghost Plug at San Onofre

location.name: San Onofre Nuclear Generating Station (SONGS) Units 2 & 3 and its 230 kV switchyard, plus the planned Imperial Valley-North of SONGS 500 kV

one_liner: Twenty-six miles from this room is a 2,246-megawatt plug that has been mostly unused since January 2012. The plan to reuse it costs $2.28 billion and won't finish until the 2030s.
problem: San Onofre was Southern California's largest power plant: 2,246 MW from two reactors. It stopped generating on Jan 31, 2012, after its new steam generators wore out early, and was retired on June 7, 2013. The reactors are being torn down, but the switchyard where it plugged into the grid is one of the few things meant to stay. The state is now spending about $2.28 billion on a 145-mile, 500 kV line from Imperial Valley to a new substation about 10 miles north of SONGS. It will take over the old San Onofre-Santiago and San Onofre-Viejo 230 kV lines, so desert solar can use the corridor the nuclear plant left behind. That is due between 2032 and 2034, so this grid connection will have gone mostly unused for over 20 years.

title: The Power Plant That Spun Without Making Power

one_liner: Nine miles from here, a 1958 power unit ran about 26 full-power hours in all of 2024. The last time this site saved the grid, it did it without making a single watt.
problem: Nine miles from Irvine on Pacific Coast Highway sits the last ocean-cooled power unit in Orange County, Unit 2 (227 MW, first operated in 1958). In 2024 it ran at a 0.30% capacity factor, roughly 26 full-power hours in the whole year, and it retires on Dec 31, 2026. When San Onofre broke in 2012, CAISO had AES turn two retired units here into giant spinning 'synchronous condensers'. They produced no electricity, only the voltage support San Onofre used to provide, and could start in under an hour instead of about 12 hours for a boiler. A 644 MW air-cooled combined-cycle plant began commercial operation on the site in June 2020. It shows how one grid connection can serve as a power plant, then a voltage stabilizer, then a modern plant.

title: 1,327 Megawatts of Grid Socket Turned Courtroom

location.name: AES Redondo Beach Generating Station (retired Dec 31, 2023), about 50-acre waterfront site at 1100 N. Harbor Dr., Redondo Beach

one_liner: A gigawatt-scale grid connection on the beach went quiet on New Year's Eve 2023. Nearly three years later, the fight over the site is in court, not on the grid.
problem: Redondo Beach's ocean-cooled gas plant (1,327 MW across Units 5-8) shut down for good on New Year's Eve 2023, after state reliability extensions kept it running past its original 2020 deadline. That left a waterfront site of about 50 acres that was built to push more than a gigawatt into the grid. Instead of new clean energy, the site has turned into a long legal fight. The owner proposed about 2,300 homes, offices, a hotel and a park, and the city fought it in court under California's 'builder's remedy' housing law. Any redevelopment also needs voter approval and must restore protected wetlands. The case shows the other path for a retired plant: its big grid connection can get tied up in land fights instead of being reused.

title: The Water Plant That Unplugs for the Grid

location.name: OCWD Groundwater Replenishment System (GWRS), Fountain Valley. On Aug 14-18 and Sept 4-5, 2020, during CAISO grid emergencies, it cut its lo

one_liner: On the night California started rolling blackouts, the plant that recycles Orange County's sewage into drinking water dropped 12 megawatts in 30 minutes, and nobody's tap ran dry.
problem: GWRS is the world's largest potable water recycling plant. It cleans Orange County sewage with microfiltration, reverse osmosis and UV/peroxide, then refills the groundwater basin that most of OC drinks from. It is also one of the largest single electric loads near Irvine, averaging about 17 MW. On August 14, 2020, California declared a Stage 3 emergency and started rotating blackouts. GWRS cut production to 15 MGD and dropped its draw to 5 MW, and it did the same again in the September heat wave. Recycled water also takes much less energy per acre-foot than imported or desalinated water. The point: water plants can act as flexible loads, and in a heatwave they can give power back to the grid.

one_liner: Making ocean water drinkable takes about four times the electricity of recycling our own wastewater, which is a big reason the state said no to a desal plant nine miles from where we're standing.

title: The Giant Battery That's Been 'Coming Soon' Since 1995

location.name: Lake Elsinore Advanced Pumped Storage (LEAPS), later renamed the Bluewater Renewable Energy Storage Project. A proposed 500 MW / 6,000 MWh p

one_liner: Twenty-seven miles from here there's a 500-megawatt water battery that could get Orange County through a heatwave evening, and it has been 'proposed' since before most of us were born.
problem: Pumped storage is a water battery. When solar power is cheap, you pump water uphill. At night or in a heatwave peak, you let it run back down through turbines. LEAPS would use Lake Elsinore as the bottom tank and a new dam in Decker Canyon as the top tank, giving 500 MW for up to 12 hours. That is about a quarter of the old San Onofre nuclear plant, enough to carry a heatwave evening. The idea dates to at least 1995. FERC dismissed the license in December 2021 and in 2023 refused even a new study permit, saying the developer had had years without progress. Lake Hodges in San Diego County shows the concept works at smaller scale: a 40 MW pumped storage plant running since 2012.

title: The Batteries Hiding Behind Irvine's Water Pumps

problem: Irvine's water utility spends a lot of electricity pumping and treating water, mostly at the most expensive hours. Starting in 2016, about 370 Tesla Powerpacks were installed at 11 of its most energy-hungry facilities: recycling plants, a deep-aquifer treatment system, a groundwater desalter and six high-energy pumping stations. The batteries charge cheaply and run the pumps during peak hours, saving IRWD more than $500,000 a year. Under a 10-year SCE contract, the batteries can also take part of the load off the grid on request. It was part of SCE's response to the San Onofre nuclear closure. The water keeps flowing the whole time.

title: Ghost Mirrors of Kramer Junction

location.name: SEGS III-VII (Solar Energy Generating Systems) solar-thermal plant at Kramer Junction, decommissioned 2021-2022 and redeveloped as Resurgenc

one_liner: California's 1980s mirror-and-steam solar plant at Kramer Junction, which also burned natural gas, was torn down and replaced on the same land by 138 megawatts of solar panels and batteries.
problem: In the 1980s the Mojave Desert hosted the SEGS complex, which used curved mirrors to boil water and could also burn natural gas. At Kramer Junction, five 30 MW SEGS units (150 MW total) fed Southern California Edison's grid. NextEra retired them in 2021 and finished decommissioning in Sept 2022. The county had already permitted the site in 2021 for solar panels plus batteries. Today USGS maps 90 MW AC (Resurgence Solar) plus 48 MW AC (Resurgence Solar II) of PV there, both online in 2023 with batteries. It is a real example of repowering an old site instead of building new.

shock_line: California's 1980s mirror-and-steam solar plant at Kramer Junction, which also burned natural gas, was torn down and replaced on the same land by 138 megawatts of solar panels and batteries.

stats.label: CEC staff memo (Sept 30, 2022): SEGS III-VII was five 30 MW solar-thermal and natural-gas-fired units generating up to 150 MW for SCE's grid. The CEC certified it in May 1988 and the facility went online in Feb 1989 (per the CEC). The site is about 500 acres one mile north of Kramer Junction.

The CEC approved the decommissioning plan on June 9, 2021, and decommissioning was complete on Sept 29, 2022. San Bernardino County issued CUPs PROJ-2021-00019 and PROJ-2021-00079 on Sept 21, 2021 to redevelop the site for solar PV and a battery energy storage system.

EIA: SEGS 3 through 7 retired in July 2021. The SEGS complex (356 MW total, nine plants) began operating in 1984. EIA's summary lists units 3-7 at 36 MW each, but the CEC says 30 MW each, so use the CEC's 150 MW total.

USGS US Large-Scale Solar PV Database: Resurgence Solar (EIA 64489), 90.0 MW AC / 108.9 MW DC, single-axis, with batteries, year 2023, at 35.0142, -117.556. Resurgence Solar II (EIA 66620), 48.0 MW AC, with batteries, year 2023. Combined PV is 138 MW AC on the former SEGS site. Note that USPVDB labels both 'greenfield' even though the site was previously developed.

title: The Renewable Highway That Went Underground in Chino Hills

location.name: Tehachapi Renewable Transmission Project (TRTP), Segment 8 500 kV underground section through Chino Hills and Chino

one_liner: Twenty-one miles from Irvine, the line built to bring Tehachapi wind into Southern California had to have its towers torn down and be buried under Chino Hills.
problem: SCE built TRTP, a 173-mile chain of new and upgraded 500 kV lines and substations, to carry up to 4,500 MW of mostly wind power from the Tehachapi area into the LA Basin. In Chino Hills, about 21 miles from Irvine, SCE had already put up overhead towers when residents fought them. In 2013 the CPUC ordered that stretch rebuilt underground. SCE demolished 16 poles and towers and installed North America's first 500 kV XLPE underground cable, roughly 3.5 to 3.7 miles long, commissioned in Oct 2016. The full line was energized in Dec 2016. Building new transmission is slow, disputed, and expensive, which is why getting more out of existing wires matters.

shock_line: Twenty-one miles from Irvine, the line built to bring Tehachapi wind into Southern California had to have its towers torn down and be buried under Chino Hills.

stats.label: SCE: TRTP can carry 4,500 MW. It comprises about 250 miles of transmission facilities across about 173 miles in 11 segments, and was fully energized in Q4 / December 2016. SCE says it serves the equivalent of about 3 million homes. Undergrounding of Segment 8 in Chino Hills began construction in summer 2014.

T&D World (Dec 19, 2016): the underground segment is 'the first North American installation of 500-kV XLPE transmission line' and the world's first 500 kV line in duct structures along steep terrain. Cables were commissioned Oct 2016, and 16 double-circuit poles and towers plus 27 foundations of the partially built overhead line were demolished. The segment uses two transition stations of about 3 acres each and is about 3.7 miles long per the CPUC ruling.
The CPUC granted Chino Hills' petition in 2013 and ordered SCE to replace the partially built 500 kV overhead line with underground facilities (CPUC addendum June 2013, about 3.5 miles).
